entry: British grime MC, rapper, record producer and DJ. He briefly joined Roll Deep with his brother Jme before founding the collective Boy Better Know. His fourth studio album, *Konnichiwa* (2016), won the Mercury Prize and featured the hit singles "That's Not Me" and "Shutdown". In 2018 he produced and featured on ASAP Rocky's single "Praise the Lord (Da Shine)", a global hit. He has been nominated for three Brit Awards, and as a key figure in the grime scene he appeared on Debrett's 2017 list of the most influential people in the UK.

Questioning attitude or doubt toward knowledge claims that are seen as mere [[Belief|belief]] or dogma. Skeptics usually recommend suspension of belief rather than disbelief, a neutral stance that neither affirms nor denies a claim, often because the evidence is insufficient. In philosophy, skepticism is a major topic in [[Epistemology|epistemology]]. Radical forms deny that knowledge or rational belief is possible, while moderate forms claim only that nothing can be known with certainty. In ancient philosophy, skepticism was a way of life associated with inner peace. Scientific skepticism tests beliefs for reliability through systematic investigation using the [[Scientific method|scientific method]], and the attitude is also applied to politics, religion and [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscience]].

Winter sport in which competitors aim for the farthest jump after sliding down a specially curved ramp on skis. Judges also score each jump's style, up to 20 points per judge, and distance is measured against the K-point, a line in the landing area that serves as a target. Technique has evolved from parallel skis with both arms extended forward to the widely used V-style. Ski jumping was first contested in [[Norway]] in the late 19th century and spread through Europe and North America in the early 20th century. It has been part of the Winter Olympics since 1924, and the first women's Olympic event was held in 2014. The sport can also be practiced in summer, on in-runs made of smooth porcelain tracks. The highest summer competition is the FIS Ski Jumping Grand Prix, contested since 1994.

Use of skis to glide on [[Snow|snow]] for basic transport, recreation or competitive sport. Skiing has a history of almost five millennia, and modern skiing evolved from beginnings in [[Scandinavia]]. It may have been practiced more than 100 centuries ago in the [[Altai Mountains]], according to an interpretation of ancient paintings, though this is debated. Skiing was used mainly for transport until the mid-19th century. Two main genres emerged as ski lifts were developed: [[Alpine skiing|alpine]] (downhill) skiing, with bindings attached at both the toe and heel, and Nordic skiing, with bindings attached only at the toe. Nordic disciplines include [[Ski jumping|ski jumping]] and cross-country skiing. Skiing has been featured at the [[Winter Olympic Games|Winter Olympics]] since 1924 for Nordic events and since 1936 for Alpine.

Learned or innate ability to act with determined results and good execution, often within a given amount of time, energy or both. Skills may be domain-general, such as time management, teamwork and self-motivation, or domain-specific, used for a particular job. Hard skills, or technical skills, relate to a specific task and can be tested and quantified, while soft skills combine people skills, communication, character traits and emotional intelligence. In his 2008 book *Outliers*, [[Malcolm Gladwell]] proposed the "10,000 hour rule": world-class skill could be developed by practicing for 10,000 hours. Other commentators disputed the rule. Social skills facilitate interaction with others, and the process of learning them is called [[Socialization|socialization]]. Skilled craft workers, such as electricians, masons and bakers, were often politically active through their guilds.

Cancer that arises from the skin, most often caused by [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] exposure. Skin cancer is the most common form of cancer, globally accounting for at least 40% of cases. The three main types are basal-cell and squamous-cell carcinomas, together called nonmelanoma skin cancer, and [[Melanoma|melanoma]], the most aggressive. More than 90% of cases are caused by ultraviolet radiation from the [[Sun|sun]]. Diagnosis is by [[Biopsy|biopsy]]. Nonmelanoma skin cancer is usually curable, mainly by surgical removal, while melanoma may be treated with surgery, [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]], [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]] or targeted therapy. More than 90% of melanoma patients in the United States survive more than five years. Decreasing ultraviolet exposure and using sunscreen appear effective at preventing melanoma and squamous-cell skin cancer.

Harmful witch in [[Navajo]] mythology who can turn into, possess or disguise itself as an animal. The Navajo term, *yee naaldlooshii*, means "by means of it, it goes on all fours." Skin-walkers are seen as the antithesis of Navajo values, performing malevolent ceremonies, and the term is never used for healers. The legend is rarely discussed with outsiders, partly because of cultural taboos. Animals associated with witchcraft usually include tricksters such as the [[Coyote (mythology)|coyote]]. Cherokee Nation academic Adrienne Keene has objected to non-Navajo writers adapting the legends, citing [[J. K. Rowling]].

Member of a working-class youth subculture that originated in [[London]] in the 1960s. Skinheads are defined by close-cropped heads and working-class clothing such as Dr. Martens [[Boot|boots]], braces and button-down shirts. The first skinheads drew on mod fashion and Jamaican music, especially [[Reggae|reggae]] and ska. A second wave in the late 1970s and early 1980s interacted with [[Punk rock|punk]] and produced Oi!. Political affiliations split the subculture into far-right and far-left strands, although many skins described themselves as apolitical. By the 1990s, neo-Nazi skinhead movements existed across [[Europe]] and [[North America]].

[[Lizard]] of the family Scincidae, one of the most diverse lizard families. With more than 1,500 described species across 100 genera, skinks are found in most habitats except arctic and subarctic regions. Most have smaller legs than typical lizards, and some genera have none. Most species have long tails that they can shed through autotomy; a lost tail can regrow within about three to four months, though imperfectly. Skinks are mainly insectivorous, eating flies, [[Cricket (insect)|crickets]], [[Grasshopper|grasshoppers]], [[Beetle|beetles]] and caterpillars. They are neither poisonous nor venomous. The oldest known skink, *Electroscincus zedi*, comes from amber in [[Myanmar]] dating to around 100 million years ago. Skinks of the genus *Prasinohaema* have green blood, from a buildup of biliverdin.

Garment covering the body from the waist or hips downward, worn as the lower part of a [[Dress|dress]] or as a separate outer garment. Most skirts are fitted at the waist and fuller below, with fullness introduced by darts, gores, pleats or panels. Hemlines range from micro to floor-length, varying with cultural ideas of modesty and with [[Fashion|fashion]]. Skirts have been worn since prehistoric times: a figurine from the Vinča culture (c. 5700–4500 BC), in present-day [[Serbia]], shows a skirt-like garment, and a straw-woven skirt dating to 3900 BC was found in [[Armenia]]. Skirts were standard attire for men and women in ancient [[Egypt]] and [[Mesopotamia]]. From the [[Middle Ages]], men increasingly wore trousers, and skirts became gendered in Western fashion as they remained standard for women.

Capital and largest city of [[North Macedonia]] (pop., 2021: 526,502), on the Vardar River. Founded as Scupi in the late 1st century during the rule of [[Domitian]], it was abandoned in 518 after an earthquake and later rebuilt under [[Justinian I]]. The [[Ottoman Empire]] ruled the city for over five centuries. After the [[Balkan Wars]], it was annexed by the Kingdom of Serbia in 1912 and became part of [[Yugoslavia]]. A major earthquake in 1963 devastated the city, which was largely rebuilt with international assistance. It became the capital of independent North Macedonia in 1991.

Bony enclosure around the [[Brain|brain]] of a [[Vertebrate|vertebrate]], forming the head. In humans, the skull is generally considered to have 22 bones: eight cranial bones that form the neurocranium around the brain, and fourteen facial bones. The bones are joined by immovable fibrous sutures. The mandible, its largest bone, articulates with the temporal bones. The skull protects the brain, anchors chewing and neck muscles, and houses the eyes, ears and nose. In some [[Fish|fish]] and amphibians it is made of cartilage. In [[Ungulate|ungulates]] and [[Elephant|elephants]], it provides the foundation for horns, antlers and tusks. The human skull fully develops two years after birth.

[[New World]] mammal of the family Mephitidae, known for spraying a strong-smelling liquid from its anal glands. All species show warning coloration, and most are black and white, though some are brown, cream or ginger. Skunks are closely related to the Old World stink badgers, and more distantly to polecats and other weasels. Most species are solitary and crepuscular when not breeding, and they shelter in burrows by day. Their diet includes insects, small vertebrates, fruits and nuts. Striped skunks range from southern Canada to northern Mexico. Threats include habitat loss, road mortality and [[Rabies|rabies]], but many populations remain stable, and skunks can live up to seven years in the wild.

Unobstructed view upward from the surface of the [[Earth]], including the atmosphere and outer space. In astronomy the sky is also called the [[Celestial sphere|celestial sphere]], an abstract sphere on which the Sun, Moon, planets and stars appear to drift. The celestial sphere is conventionally divided into [[Constellation|constellations]]. The daytime sky appears blue because air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of sunlight more than longer ones, a process known as [[Rayleigh scattering]]. The night sky appears as a mostly dark surface spangled with stars. Natural phenomena seen in the sky include [[Rainbow|rainbows]], [[Aurora|auroras]] and [[Lightning|lightning]]. Smog and light pollution are often seen above large cities.

First space station launched by [[NASA]], occupied by three crews for about 24 weeks between May 1973 and February 1974. Built from a repurposed third stage of the [[Saturn V]] rocket, it was launched uncrewed and served as a workshop and solar observatory. It was the world's second space station, after the Soviet space program's Salyut 1. Its pressurized volume of over 350 m³ was not exceeded until [[Mir]] was completed in 1996. Plans to reuse it with the [[Space Shuttle]] were abandoned, and it disintegrated in the atmosphere on July 11, 1979, scattering debris across the [[Indian Ocean]] and Western Australia.

Former telecommunications application for internet video calls, voice calls and instant messaging, retired in 2025. Skype was founded in 2003 by Niklas Zennström and Janus Friis, with four developers from [[Estonia]]. [[EBay|eBay]] bought it in 2005 for $2.6 billion. In 2011, [[Microsoft]] bought it for $8.5 billion and used it to replace its Windows Live Messenger. In 2017 the service moved from a peer-to-peer system to a centralized, Azure-based service. It was retired on May 5, 2025, and its website redirects users to Microsoft Teams.

Very tall, permanently habitable building, typically at least 150 m (492 ft) high. Most skyscrapers have a steel frame with curtain walls that are supported by the framework rather than bearing load. Modern examples often have a tubular structure that acts like a hollow cylinder to resist wind and seismic loads. Skyscrapers first emerged at the end of the 19th century, especially in [[New York City]] and [[Chicago]]. Construction slowed sharply during the [[Great Depression]] and did not fully resume until the 1950s. A boom in East and Southeast [[Asia]] began in the 1990s, and more than three quarters of skyscrapers taller than 150 m are in Asia. The [[Burj Khalifa]] in [[Dubai]], at 828 m (2,717 ft), is the tallest. [[Hong Kong]] has the most skyscrapers, with 569.

[[Vocabulary]] of an informal register, common in everyday conversation but avoided in formal writing and speech. The term also refers to the language used by members of particular in-groups to establish identity and exclude outsiders. The earliest attested use, in 1756, referred to the vocabulary of "low" or "disreputable" people. The word was first used in print around 1800 to describe the language of London's criminal classes. Linguists have no simple definition of slang, and it is generally seen as a constantly changing feature of every subculture. Unlike colloquial terms, which are broadly acceptable, slang tends to be seen as inappropriate in many communication situations. Slang differs from jargon, which optimizes communication among specialists, though the two terms are sometimes treated as synonymous.

Slanting line punctuation mark (/), also called a stroke or solidus. Once used as the equivalent of the modern [[Full stop|period]] and comma, the slash now represents [[Division (mathematics)|division]] and [[Fraction|fractions]], separates alternative or related terms, and serves as a date separator and an abbreviation mark. It derives from the medieval virgule, a mark used as a full stop. In the 18th century it was generally known in English as the "oblique," and the name "slash" became widespread through its use in computing.

[[Horror film|Horror]] subgenre in which a killer or group of killers stalks and murders people, often with bladed or sharp tools. Critics cite the psychological horror of *Peeping Tom* (1960), *Psycho* (1960), directed by [[Alfred Hitchcock]], and Italian giallo films as early influences. The genre peaked between 1978 and 1984, its "Golden Age," with *Halloween* (1978), directed by [[John Carpenter]]. The typical heroine is the "final girl," such as [[Jamie Lee Curtis]]'s Laurie Strode in *Halloween*. Films with non-human antagonists, such as *Alien* or *The Terminator*, are not traditionally considered slashers.

Fine-grained, foliated metamorphic rock formed from [[Shale|shale]]-type sedimentary rock by low-grade regional metamorphism. Its slaty cleavage develops as compression realigns fine clay minerals into planes perpendicular to the pressure. Slate splits into smooth, flat sheets, so it has long been used for [[Roof|roofing]], floor tiles and billiard tables. It is mainly composed of [[Quartz|quartz]], illite and chlorite, with iron oxides such as [[Hematite|hematite]], [[Magnetite|magnetite]] and [[Pyrite|pyrite]]. Slate is frequently grey, but it can be purple, green or cyan, as in North Wales. It is not to be confused with shale or [[Schist|schist]]. Global output exceeds 200 million tonnes annually as of 2020, with major production in Spain, [[China]] and India.

Anti-war novel by [[Kurt Vonnegut]], published in 1969, that blends semi-autobiography with [[Science fiction|science fiction]]. Its protagonist, Billy Pilgrim, is an American chaplain's assistant in [[World War II]] who fights in the [[Battle of the Bulge]], is captured in 1944, and survives the Allied firebombing of [[Dresden]] as a prisoner of war. Billy becomes "unstuck in time," and the nonlinear structure mirrors his psychological trauma. Vonnegut drew on an experience he endured as an American serviceman. The novel was nominated for the Hugo and Nebula Awards but lost to [[Ursula K. Le Guin]]'s *The Left Hand of Darkness*.

Systems of servitude that were widespread in historical Africa, both indigenous and for export. Slavery was part of African economic structures for centuries. Local slave systems began supplying captives to the trans-Saharan, [[Red Sea]], [[Indian Ocean]] and [[Atlantic slave trade]] markets. Indigenous forms included debt slavery, enslavement of war captives, military slavery and enslavement of criminals. In many communities, slaves increased a master's influence and connections, and children of slaves could rise to prominent positions, even chief. [[Ibn Battuta]] visited [[Mali]] in the mid-14th century and was given a slave boy as a "hospitality gift." Chattel slavery has a long documented history in the [[Nile]] valley, the [[Sahel]] and North Africa. The transatlantic trade, peaking from the 16th to 19th centuries, exported about 12.5 million Africans. Earlier Arab-oriented trades across the Sahara and East Africa were estimated at 10 to 18 million over 1,200 years, though figures are debated.

Legal institution of chattel slavery, mostly in the South, prevalent in the United States from its founding in 1776 until 1865. Children were born into slavery, and enslaved people were treated as property that could be bought, sold or given away. Congress banned the [[Atlantic slave trade]] in 1808, but smuggling continued. Cotton expansion after the [[Cotton gin|cotton gin]] greatly increased demand for labor in the [[Deep South]], and the enslaved population reached four million. After [[Abraham Lincoln]] won the 1860 election, slave states seceded and the [[American Civil War]] began. The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified December 6, 1865, prohibited slavery except as punishment for crime.

Subfamily of [[Indo-European languages]] spoken primarily by the Slavic peoples and their descendants. They descend from Proto-Slavic, spoken in the Early Middle Ages, which in turn descended from Proto-Balto-Slavic and is linked to the Baltic languages. They are spoken across the [[Balkans]], Central and Eastern Europe, and from western [[Siberia]] to the Russian Far East. About 315 million people spoke them at the turn of the 21st century, making them the largest ethnolinguistic group in Europe. They are conventionally divided into East, South and West branches. Of more than 20 languages, 10 have at least one million speakers and national status, including Russian, Polish, Bulgarian and [[Serbo-Croatian]]. Most are highly inflectional, with three genders and usually subject–verb–object word order.
